correct_answer: The reduced root radius (1.8mm per P&W Drawing Rev F) combined with die wear at the root cavity created a stress concentration; the Excel maintenance log noting 'hairline wear mark at root cavity' in July 2025 was the earliest actionable signal that should have triggered die replacement before the August production run
rationale: The correct answer requires tracing through six systems: (1) S/4HANA quality notification identifies the defect location (dovetail root); (2) the batch classification Z-field traces back to legacy MAT-44120-A; (3) the SharePoint consolidation mapping identifies that MAT-44120-A is the modified root radius variant; (4) MasterControl shows the root radius was reduced from 2.5mm to 1.8mm; (5) the Teams conversation connects the legacy material to the cracking location; and critically (6) the Excel maintenance log — the least formal source — shows die wear was observed at the root cavity a month before the defective batch was produced, within the same die set (DS-2022-003). The thinner root radius made the part more sensitive to die wear-induced surface defects that nucleate fatigue cracks. Answer A incorrectly blames the migration itself rather than the underlying manufacturing condition. Answer C deflects responsibility by pointing to the customer spec, ignoring that Ironforge's die maintenance is their process control obligation regardless of geometry. Answer D unnecessarily delays investigation when sufficient traceability exists through the Z-field and mapping table.
